name: Chapter 6: Analyzing financial statements: Profitability, growth, and liquidity

questions.text: What is return on assets (ROA) intended to measure?

options.a: Cash holdings relative to current liabilities
options.b: Revenue generated relative to equity market capitalization
options.c: Dividends paid relative to total assets
options.d: Net income generated relative to the average total asset base

questions.text: Why does ROA combine information from two primary financial statements?

options.a: It compares only share prices and dividends
options.b: Both the numerator and denominator are financing cash flows
options.c: The numerator is a measure of earnings and the denominator is a balance-sheet asset measure
options.d: It compares only two income-statement expenses

questions.text: What is the formula for ROA used in the lecture?

options.a: Net income divided by average shareholders' equity
options.b: EBIT divided by interest expense
options.c: Revenue divided by average inventory
options.d: Net income divided by average total assets

questions.text: What is return on equity (ROE)?

options.a: Current assets divided by current liabilities
options.b: Net income divided by average shareholders' equity
options.c: Operating cash flow divided by sales
options.d: Sales divided by total PPE

questions.text: Which perspective does ROE emphasize?

options.a: Returns associated with the owners' equity capital
options.b: Inventory purchased relative to sales
options.c: The coupon rate earned by bondholders
options.d: Customer credit risk exclusively

questions.text: Why should the denominator of ROE commonly use average equity rather than only year-end equity?

options.a: Average equity is always identical to year-end equity
options.b: Only year-end shares legally generate profits
options.c: Income is earned over a period whereas equity is a stock measured at specific dates
options.d: The closing equity balance is never disclosed

questions.text: What is ROCE as defined specifically in this lecture chapter?

options.a: Return on total capital employed before tax in every context
options.b: Return on common shareholders' equity attributable to parent common shareholders
options.c: Revenue on cash equivalents
options.d: Return on current expenses

questions.text: Why must non-controlling interests be excluded when computing parent-common-shareholder ROCE?

options.a: All subsidiaries are wholly owned
options.b: Non-controlling interests belong to the parent shareholders
options.c: The numerator and denominator should reflect the same owners' income and equity
options.d: Non-controlling interests are always cash equivalents

questions.text: What is the traditional two-factor DuPont identity?

options.a: ROA = Dividend yield × Price-to-book
options.b: ROE = DSO × DPO
options.c: ROE = ROA × Financial leverage
options.d: ROE = Gross margin + Current ratio

questions.text: How is financial leverage defined in the lecture's DuPont model?

options.a: Average inventory divided by sales
options.b: Net income divided by total assets
options.c: Average total assets divided by average shareholders' equity
options.d: Current liabilities divided by current assets

questions.text: What is the main trade-off in increasing financial leverage?

options.a: It can magnify equity returns but also increase financial distress risk
options.b: It guarantees a higher operating return on assets
options.c: It automatically lowers interest expenses
options.d: It reduces all contractual obligations

questions.text: For positive ROA, what is the algebraic effect of greater asset-to-equity leverage, other things equal?

options.a: ROE increases
options.b: ROE becomes negative immediately
options.c: ROE becomes independent of assets
options.d: ROE must equal zero

questions.text: For negative ROA, what does an increase in positive financial leverage do, all else equal?

options.a: It guarantees a positive ROE
options.b: It magnifies the negative ROE
options.c: It makes net income positive
options.d: It eliminates equity losses

questions.text: Why does high ROE not necessarily indicate strong underlying operations?

options.a: ROE never depends on financing structure
options.b: A high ROE always indicates low bankruptcy risk
options.c: ROE is based exclusively on customer receipts
options.d: It may partly reflect a small equity base and high leverage

questions.text: What does the three-part DuPont decomposition express?

options.a: ROE = Net profit margin × Asset turnover × Financial leverage
options.b: ROE = Cash ratio × Dividend payout
options.c: ROE = DSO + DIO - DPO
options.d: ROE = EBIT + Depreciation + Amortization

questions.text: What is net profit margin?

options.a: Cost of goods sold divided by inventory
options.b: Dividends per share divided by price
options.c: Sales divided by average total assets
options.d: Net income divided by sales

questions.text: What is asset turnover?

options.a: Sales divided by average total assets
options.b: Net income divided by average shareholders' equity
options.c: Gross interest expense divided by EBIT
options.d: Cash divided by accounts receivable

questions.text: What happens to ROA if net profit margin increases and asset turnover stays constant?

options.a: ROA increases
options.b: ROA decreases
options.c: ROA becomes equal to the interest rate
options.d: ROA cannot change

questions.text: What does a low asset turnover combined with a high profit margin often suggest?

options.a: A firm that necessarily has no fixed assets
options.b: A capital-intensive or differentiated business that earns more profit per sale
options.c: A firm with certain insolvency
options.d: A company selling only on credit

questions.text: Why should analysts examine both profit margin and asset turnover?

options.a: Asset turnover is mathematically identical to gross margin
options.b: Profit margin never depends on operating expenses
options.c: Different combinations can produce the same ROA
options.d: Both are measures of outstanding debt only

questions.text: What is gross profit margin?

options.a: Net income divided by average PPE
options.b: Cash from operations divided by sales
options.c: Net income divided by shareholders' equity
options.d: Gross profit divided by sales

questions.text: What may cause gross margin to decline?

options.a: An unconditional increase in pricing power
options.b: Higher input costs, stronger competition, lower volumes, or adverse product mix
options.c: An automatic increase in inventory turnover
options.d: A guaranteed decline in cost of goods sold

questions.text: How should an operating-expense-to-sales margin generally be interpreted?

options.a: It measures operating costs incurred per euro of revenue
options.b: It represents all marketable securities
options.c: It directly measures the amount of cash held in bank accounts
options.d: It is an interest coverage ratio

questions.text: How can expense-margin analysis help explain a change in net profit margin?

options.a: It identifies future stock returns exactly
options.b: It eliminates every difference between industries
options.c: It replaces revenue recognition policies
options.d: It identifies which operating cost categories rose or fell relative to sales

questions.text: Why may two firms have similar ROA but very different asset structures?

options.a: Higher margin can offset lower asset turnover and vice versa
options.b: They must have identical inventory and PPE balances
options.c: ROA fixes an identical depreciation schedule
options.d: Asset turnover is unrelated to assets

questions.text: Which ratio directly reveals the efficiency of trade-receivables use within asset turnover analysis?

options.a: Debt-to-equity ratio exclusively
options.b: Times interest earned
options.c: Dividend payout ratio
options.d: Accounts receivable turnover

questions.text: Why can goodwill impairments change measured asset turnover even when sales are stable?

options.a: A lower carrying value of total assets can raise turnover mechanically
options.b: Asset turnover does not use assets in its denominator
options.c: Goodwill impairment always increases sales
options.d: Goodwill is always excluded from total assets

questions.text: What is sales growth?

options.a: Current-period sales divided by previous-period sales, minus one
options.b: Net income divided by shareholders' equity
options.c: Operating cash flow divided by total debt
options.d: Current assets divided by current liabilities

questions.text: What is earnings growth?

options.a: Dividend yield multiplied by share price
options.b: Current-period earnings divided by prior-period earnings, minus one
options.c: PPE divided by sales
options.d: Revenue divided by average inventory

questions.text: What is the difficulty in interpreting simple earnings-growth percentages when prior-year earnings are near zero or negative?

options.a: A negative base guarantees strong sustainable growth
options.b: The formula cannot be affected by prior-year earnings
options.c: Growth percentages always remain between 0% and 100%
options.d: The percentage can be extremely volatile or economically misleading

questions.text: What are sustainable earnings?

options.a: A market value equal to all outstanding debt
options.b: Any unusually large one-time gain
options.c: Earnings generated solely by asset disposal
options.d: Earnings likely to persist and potentially grow from recurring business performance

questions.text: What other term does the lecture use for sustainable earnings?

options.a: Core or persistent earnings
options.b: Financing cash flow
options.c: Contingent liabilities
options.d: Unearned share capital

questions.text: What are transitory earnings items?

options.a: Non-recurring or unusual gains and losses that are unlikely to persist
options.b: The firm's most stable recurring margins
options.c: Dividends paid each year
options.d: Only sales from its largest product

questions.text: Why does analyzing sustainable earnings require understanding competitive advantage?

options.a: Sustainable earnings depend only on depreciation methods
options.b: All competitive advantages last forever
options.c: Profit persistence is independent of strategy
options.d: Competition can erode returns and make apparent growth difficult to maintain

questions.text: How can delayed recognition of deferred revenue affect the apparent earnings-growth path?

options.a: Deferred revenue is always recognized immediately as profit
options.b: Deferred revenue cannot change reported net income
options.c: Moving revenue recognition between periods can distort reported growth
options.d: Advance customer payments are dividends

questions.text: Why is an increase in deferred revenue not automatically an increase in current-period profit?

options.a: Deferred revenue is an equity investment
options.b: A cash receipt is always an earned sale
options.c: The firm still owes goods or services and has not yet earned the revenue
options.d: Every customer prepayment creates a capital gain

questions.text: How could excessive restructuring provisions lead to artificial future earnings growth?

options.a: Provisions are always unrelated to profit
options.b: Restructuring charges always raise current-year profit
options.c: The firm cannot reverse any estimated liability under any circumstances
options.d: Subsequent reversals or lower future charges may make later earnings appear unusually strong

questions.text: Which is an example of a restructuring-related charge?

options.a: An ordinary customer deposit
options.b: Cash received from issuing shares
options.c: Revenue from recurring product sales
options.d: Employee severance costs

questions.text: Why should an analyst scrutinize a sudden reduction in R&D or advertising expenditure?

options.a: It always signals higher future sales growth
options.b: It means every remaining research project is successful
options.c: It has no effect on current reported expenses
options.d: It can improve current profit while damaging future competitive performance

questions.text: What does sustainable-earnings growth compare?

options.a: Current interest expense with prior assets
options.b: Estimated recurring earnings in the current and prior periods
options.c: Dividend yield and market capitalization
options.d: Opening and closing cash balances exclusively

questions.text: Which indicator is most directly related to the short-term payment capacity of a firm?

options.a: Liquidity
options.b: Patent grants
options.c: Weighted-average shares outstanding
options.d: Gross margin

questions.text: Which difference of balance-sheet amounts defines net working capital in liquidity analysis?

options.a: Sales minus cost of goods sold
options.b: Current assets minus current liabilities
options.c: Net debt divided by EBITDA
options.d: Net income plus depreciation

questions.text: What is the current ratio?

options.a: Current assets divided by current liabilities
options.b: EBIT divided by interest expense
options.c: Cash divided by total equity
options.d: Current liabilities divided by current assets

questions.text: What is the quick ratio as defined in the lecture?

options.a: Inventories divided by current assets
options.b: Cash plus cash equivalents plus accounts receivable, divided by current liabilities
options.c: Total current assets including inventory divided by non-current debt
options.d: Sales divided by current liabilities

questions.text: Why does the quick ratio exclude inventories?

options.a: Inventory always has a guaranteed selling price
options.b: Inventory is never included in current assets
options.c: Inventory may be less readily convertible into cash without losses or delays
options.d: Inventory is a financing activity

questions.text: What is the cash ratio?

options.a: Cash and cash equivalents divided by current liabilities
options.b: Current liabilities divided by total assets
options.c: Inventory divided by trade payables
options.d: Net income divided by cash

questions.text: Which ratio is the most restrictive measure of immediate liquid-asset coverage among current, quick, and cash ratios?

options.a: Inventory turnover
options.b: Gross profit margin
options.c: Current ratio
options.d: Cash ratio

questions.text: What does a times-interest-earned ratio assess?

options.a: Current assets held per new patent
options.b: Cash conversion of ordinary share dividends
options.c: EBIT coverage of gross interest expense
options.d: Inventory held per euro of sales

questions.text: Why may times-interest-earned overstate near-term debt-service capacity?

options.a: It includes every required loan repayment in the denominator
options.b: It uses cash payments only
options.c: It excludes all interest expenses
options.d: EBIT is accrual-based and the ratio ignores principal repayments

questions.text: What does operating cash flow to total debt assess?

options.a: Employee headcount relative to inventories
options.b: Current gross profit relative to sales
options.c: Cash-generating ability relative to total interest-bearing debt
options.d: Dividend payments relative to market price

questions.text: Why deduct capital expenditure in adjusted CFO-to-debt analysis?

options.a: Capex is always an interest receipt
options.b: Capex creates immediate net income
options.c: Debt is always a non-cash expense
options.d: Some operating cash is committed to necessary investment before it can service debt

questions.text: What is EBITDA?

options.a: Estimated book value of all assets
options.b: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization
options.c: Earnings before inventory turnover and dividend allocation
options.d: Equity before intangible debt and acquisitions

questions.text: Why do analysts use EBITDA-based interest coverage?

options.a: EBITDA includes debt principal repayments
options.b: EBITDA deducts all working-capital outflows automatically
options.c: Depreciation and amortization are non-cash charges, so adding them back provides another earnings-based coverage view
options.d: EBITDA is identical to actual operating cash flow under all conditions

questions.text: What is a major limitation of EBITDA as a proxy for cash flow?

options.a: It is defined as cash received from customers
options.b: It excludes working-capital changes and capital expenditure needs
options.c: It measures market value of equity directly
options.d: It includes all cash investment spending

questions.text: What is the purpose of Altman's original Z-score model?

options.a: Forecasting the market price of every ordinary share precisely
options.b: Combining financial ratios to help predict bankruptcy or financial distress
options.c: Pricing convertible bonds without assumptions
options.d: Measuring only environmental emissions

questions.text: Which input is part of the classic Altman Z-score presented in the slides?

options.a: R&D patents divided by employees
options.b: Working capital divided by total assets
options.c: Dividend payout divided by cash
options.d: Customer satisfaction divided by sales

questions.text: Which market-based indicator is included in the original Altman Z-score for public manufacturing firms?

options.a: Number of new products per employee
options.b: Cash dividends per share relative to revenue
options.c: Market value of equity relative to total liabilities
options.d: Share repurchases divided by cost of goods sold

questions.text: According to the slide's Z-score interpretation, what does a score below 1.80 suggest?

options.a: That the firm is always in a mature lifecycle stage
options.b: Elevated financial-distress and bankruptcy risk
options.c: A guaranteed absence of financial distress
options.d: High future stock-market returns

questions.text: According to the lecture, what does a Z-score above 3 typically indicate?

options.a: A negative working-capital requirement
options.b: Relatively low short-term bankruptcy risk under the original model
options.c: No need to inspect financial statements
options.d: Certain bankruptcy within one year

questions.text: Why should a classic Altman Z-score be used cautiously outside its original setting?

options.a: It automatically corrects all cross-industry differences
options.b: It incorporates every non-financial risk indicator
options.c: It is a legal determination of bankruptcy
options.d: Its coefficients and cutoffs were designed for a specific population and may not generalize

questions.text: What is a limitation of comparing ratios before and after a merger?

options.a: Acquisitions may change the consolidated business mix and measurement base
options.b: A merger always preserves accounting comparability
options.c: Ratios are immune to changes in business scope
options.d: Mergers cannot affect reported assets

questions.text: Why is a ratio insufficient on its own to judge performance?

options.a: It compresses complex strategy, accounting choices, and business conditions into one number
options.b: It eliminates the need for trend analysis
options.c: It captures every qualitative aspect of operations
options.d: All industries have identical benchmark ratios

questions.text: Why might a company with very high net income still face financial distress?

options.a: Positive net income guarantees all loans are repaid
options.b: Profit need not translate into enough near-term cash to pay obligations
options.c: Working capital never affects liquidity
options.d: Financial distress can arise only when gross margin is negative

questions.text: What does deteriorating DSO combined with falling liquidity ratios suggest?

options.a: Receivable collections may be weakening and tying up cash
options.b: Immediate improvement in credit quality is guaranteed
options.c: Asset turnover must rise automatically
options.d: Suppliers are necessarily offering longer payment terms

questions.text: Why is the choice of comparable peers important in margin and turnover analysis?

options.a: Peer comparison automatically determines intrinsic equity value
options.b: Ratios are completely invariant to accounting policies
options.c: Operating models, accounting choices, and capital intensity vary across businesses
options.d: All listed firms operate in the same market

questions.text: Why do analyst adjustments for unusual items require skepticism?

options.a: Adjustments eliminate all forecasting uncertainty
options.b: Unusual losses never convey economic information
options.c: Some supposedly non-recurring expenses may recur, while adjustments can be subjective
options.d: Management adjustments are always identical to audited net income

questions.text: Two firms both earn €20 million on average assets of €200 million. Firm A has €100 million average equity, while Firm B has €50 million. Which conclusion follows from DuPont's two-factor identity?

options.a: Both firms necessarily have the same ROE
options.b: Firm B has the higher ROE because it uses greater leverage
options.c: Firm A has the higher ROE because its equity is larger
options.d: Firm B has lower ROA because its equity is smaller

questions.text: A company reports a net profit margin of 4% and asset turnover of 1.5. What is its ROA under the simple DuPont formulation?
A firm's gross margin falls while SG&A-to-sales and R&D-to-sales stay unchanged. Which explanation should be examined first?

options.a: Only the maturity of its bonds
options.b: Only the number of ordinary shares
options.c: Selling prices, product mix, or costs of goods sold
options.d: Only its dividend policy

questions.text: An analyst sees high ROE coupled with low ROA and a high asset-to-equity ratio. What is the most defensible interpretation?

options.a: The return is independent of financing choices
options.b: Leverage is an important contributor to ROE and raises risk
options.c: The firm must have superior operating margins
options.d: The firm has no financial liabilities

questions.text: A firm raises reported earnings by sharply cutting R&D while its product pipeline deteriorates. Which earnings-quality concern is most relevant?

options.a: The firm has created additional acquired goodwill
options.b: All cost reductions necessarily improve sustainable earnings
options.c: Current earnings may be temporarily inflated at the expense of future growth
options.d: Its cash conversion cycle must become negative

questions.text: A company has current assets of €100 million, including €35 million inventory, and current liabilities of €80 million. Ignoring other exclusions, why could the quick ratio be below one despite a current ratio above one?

options.a: The cash ratio adds inventories back
options.b: The quick ratio divides by long-term liabilities
options.c: The current ratio always excludes receivables
options.d: The quick ratio excludes inventory, reducing its numerator

questions.text: A firm has a classic Altman Z-score of 1.5. Which assessment aligns with the slide's thresholds?

options.a: It proves legal insolvency has already occurred
options.b: It guarantees default within 24 hours
options.c: It falls in the distress range, though further contextual analysis is required
options.d: It is automatically in the healthy zone
